subject: Copywriting
title: Personalization in Subject Lines
description: A quick win: understand Personalization in Subject Lines.

hook.text: Emails with the recipient's first name in the subject line get 26% higher open rates. A name demands attention.

buildup.text: The cocktail party effect: you hear your name across a noisy room. The same happens scanning a crowded inbox.

discovery.text: Beyond names, personal data works: 'Your flight to Paris' beats 'Flight confirmation.' Specificity signals relevance.

twist.text: Overuse killed personalization. 'Hey {First_Name}!' feels robotic now.

climax.text: The best personalization references behavior: 'You viewed this 3 times.' Behavioral data is the new first name.

punchline.text: Names work. Behavior data works better. Personalize with actions.

quiz.question: How much do personalized subject lines boost open rates?

details.summary: Adding the recipient's name or other personal data to subject lines can increase open rates by 20-30%. But personalization goes beyond {FIRST_NAME} — referencing past behavior, location, or preferences creates much deeper relevance. Over-personalization, however, can feel invasive and erode trust.
details.whyItMatters: Personalization signals relevance in a crowded inbox. Understanding the spectrum from basic name insertion to behavioral targeting helps writers find the right level.
takeaways: Name personalization increases open rates by 20-30% on average
Behavioral personalization outperforms simple name insertion
Excessive personalization can feel creepy and damage brand trust

faq.question: How much personalization is too much in email?
faq.answer: The line is crossed when the email reveals knowledge the subscriber doesn't expect you to have. Using their name or referencing a purchase feels natural. Mentioning browsing behavior they thought was private feels invasive. Match personalization depth to relationship depth.

faq.question: Does first-name personalization still work?
faq.answer: Yes, but its effectiveness has decreased as it has become ubiquitous. Subscribers are used to seeing their name in subject lines. More sophisticated personalization — referencing their last purchase, their city, or their content preferences — now produces larger lifts.
